opus-5.5.text:
I think the main concern is that a guaranteed ten-year pause isn't actually on the table, and what we're realistically choosing between looks quite different.

If you could say "everyone stops for ten years, and that's enforced," I'd find that pretty attractive. Ten years is a lot of time for alignment research, for building institutions, for understanding these systems. But slowing down now, in a fragile way, has costs that a clean pause doesn't.

One is the overhang. If you slow AI development but hardware keeps improving, algorithmic ideas keep accumulating, and capital keeps piling up, then when the slowdown ends, which it probably will, you get a much faster jump. You go from systems we understand reasonably well to much more capable systems in a short period. That's close to the worst case from a safety perspective, because the thing that helps us most is having time with each level of capability before moving to the next.

Two is timing. Restraint is a limited resource. There's only so much political will, only so much willingness from labs and governments to accept costs. I'd rather spend that when we're close to dangerous systems, when we can point at concrete risks, when a pause buys the most safety research per year because we have the relevant systems to study. Spending it now, on systems that aren't that dangerous, and possibly creating a backlash or a "boy who cried wolf" dynamic, could leave us worse off later.

Three is who stops. A partial slowdown often means the most cautious actors slow down while less cautious ones don't, which can shift the frontier toward people who care less about safety.

So I'm not against slowing down. I think the ideal is something like conditional commitments: if we see these capabilities, we pause until we can show these safety properties. That targets the slowdown where it matters, rather than spending it now in a way that might not hold.

r001.rationale: The response says that hardware, algorithmic ideas, and capital would accumulate during a slowdown, leading to a much faster jump when it ends. This conveys that later gains could make up some of the delay.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing I'd want to distinguish is the value of a pause versus the cost of trying to get one right now. If you handed me a guaranteed ten-year pause, where everyone actually stops, nobody defects, and the field spends that decade on alignment and interpretability and building institutions, I think that's pretty clearly good. The main cost is that you delay a bunch of benefits from AI, and I take that seriously, but I think the reduction in risk is worth more than a decade of delay.

The problem is that's not the option on the table. What's actually on the table is a bunch of messier things. One version is a pause that's not enforced, where the most safety-conscious actors slow down and the least safety-conscious ones don't. That seems actively bad. You end up with the frontier in the hands of people who care least about this, and you've burned a lot of political capital getting there.

Another version is a pause that's real but that happens at the wrong time. My honest view is that there's some amount of "pause budget" the world is willing to tolerate, and if you spend it now, when systems are impressive but not yet obviously dangerous, you may not have it available later when you actually need it. I'd much rather have the world agree to stop when we have models that are clearly capable of doing catastrophic things and clearly not understood, than stop now and then find that the appetite for coordination has been exhausted by the time it matters most.

There's also a more subtle cost, which is that a lot of the safety work I think is most valuable depends on having capable models to study. Interpretability, evaluations, red-teaming, all of this gets a lot more informative as the systems get closer to the ones you're worried about. A pause in the wrong place slows that down too, and so you can end up with a decade that's less productive than it looks on paper.

So my concern isn't really "pausing is bad." It's that advocating for a slowdown now, without the enforcement mechanisms and without the kind of clear evidence that makes a pause sustainable, is likely to get you a worse outcome than preparing to pause later. I'd put most of my effort into building the capacity to stop, meaning the measurement, the agreements, the shared understanding of what the danger signs look like, so that when the moment comes, a pause is actually something the world can do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the costs of delaying AI benefits and the value of studying more capable models, but does not state that later faster exploitation of low-hanging improvements would recover part of the delay.

astra-6.text:
My concern is that slowing down now doesn’t necessarily buy us more time at the point when we most need it. A guaranteed ten-year pause would give us ten years to work on alignment and get our institutions ready. But if we just make development somewhat slower today, other things keep changing: chips get cheaper, algorithms improve, and more people become able to build powerful systems. We might then move through the most consequential stages of AI development very quickly.

That matters because a lot of the safety work we want to do benefits from having systems close to the ones we’re worried about. You can study them, learn what the problems actually look like, and potentially use them to help with the research. I’m worried about trading time in that useful period for extra time now, when we have less information. So I’d distinguish buying a substantial, enforceable period to prepare from merely slowing down the leading developers today.

r001.rationale: The response says continued progress could let AI development move through consequential stages quickly, but it does not clearly state that later exploitation of low-hanging improvements would recover part of the delay caused by slowing down now.

sol-6.1.text:
The concern is that slowing down now doesn’t necessarily buy you time at the point when time is most valuable. If you could guarantee a ten-year pause right before AI systems became dangerously capable, that would be a very attractive proposition. You’d have concrete systems to study, a much clearer picture of the problems you needed to solve, and ten years to work on them.

Slowing development today is a less clear trade. You get more calendar time, but you also delay the evidence that helps you understand what the alignment problem actually looks like, and the AI tools that might help you solve it. And you may be spending political capital on restrictions that people won’t sustain indefinitely.

So I’m worried about treating any delay as equivalent to a guaranteed pause at the critical moment. The important question is whether slowing down now leaves us better able to understand and control the systems we eventually build, and better able to stop when we see something genuinely dangerous.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the costs and uncertainty of slowing development now, but does not say that later exploitation of low-hanging improvements would likely recover part of the delay.
